paragraphs.source_en: At the pillow-side of the master's wife there stood, neatly placed, a nailed-up rectangular wooden box about a foot and a half long. Inside it were yams, brought back as a local gift by Tatara Sanpei, a native of Karatsu in Hizen Province, when he returned home the other day. It is unusual enough to arrange yams by one's pillow, but this wife was the sort who would put refined cooking sugar into her sewing box. She had no notion whatever of what belonged where and what did not, so to her, not only yams but even pickled radish in the bedroom would have caused no concern. But this gentleman of the upper beams, lacking the gift of prophecy, could hardly know what our mistress was like; and since it had been set so ceremoniously beside her pillow, it was no wonder he took it for something valuable. The burglar lifted the box of yams slightly; its solid weight suited his expectations, and he appeared highly satisfied with its heft. When I thought that he really meant to steal yams, and that this handsome fellow was the very man stealing them, I suddenly found it funny. However, it would not do to burst out laughing; to avoid danger, I could only hold it in with all my might.

paragraphs.source_en: Presently the burglar began respectfully wrapping the box of yams in a blanket, and looked around for something with which to tie the bundle. Just then, fortunately, the crepe sash the master had taken off when going to bed was lying nearby. The burglar tied the box firmly with this sash and slung it easily onto his back, in a posture no woman would admire. Then he stuffed two of the children's padded vests into the master's cotton drawers, so that the legs swelled round like a rat snake that had swallowed a frog, or perhaps more aptly like a rat snake near its delivery; in any case it was an unseemly sight. If you doubt it, you might try it yourself. The burglar wound the cotton drawers around his neck; as I watched what he would do next, he spread out the master's pongee coat like a large wrapping cloth, then neatly folded into it the master's wife's sash, the master's haori, under-robe, and all manner of odds and ends. I could not help admiring his skill and thoroughness. After that he joined together the master's wife's obi-age and sash-cord and the like, tied up the bundle with them, and carried it in one hand. He looked around again to see whether there was anything else worthy of being humbly received. Finding a packet of Asahi cigarettes near the master's head, he at once tossed it into his sleeve, then took it out again, drew one cigarette from it, and lit it at the kerosene lamp. He took a deep, savoring puff, and before the smoke he exhaled had finished curling around the milky lamp chimney, the burglar's footsteps had already receded down the veranda and disappeared. The master and his wife were still sound asleep. Human beings, it seems, are unexpectedly careless creatures.
